questions.question: What happens if `Duck` implements `IFlyable` but forgets to write a `Fly()` method?
options: Nothing — Fly() just does nothing at runtime
A compile error — the contract is not fulfilled
A runtime exception the first time Fly() is called
IFlyable silently provides a default
questions.explanation: An interface is a compile-time contract. If a class claims `: IFlyable` but doesn't implement everything the interface requires, the code doesn't compile at all.

questions.question: Which is true about a class's relationship to interfaces vs. base classes?
options: A class can have one base class and implement multiple interfaces
A class can have multiple base classes but only one interface
A class can have multiple base classes and multiple interfaces
A class can have exactly one of either, never both
questions.explanation: C# has single inheritance for classes (one base class only) but a class can implement as many interfaces as needed — `class Duck : Animal, IFlyable, ISwimmable` is valid.

questions.question: What's wrong with this?
options: Nothing, this is fine
Abstract classes cannot be instantiated directly with `new`
Area() needs a body
Shape needs a constructor
questions.explanation: `abstract` on a class means it can never be `new`'d directly — it exists only to be inherited from. Only a concrete (non-abstract) subclass that implements `Area()` can be instantiated.

questions.question: Two completely unrelated classes, `Invoice` and `Employee`, both need to be processed in the same loop and summed by an `Amount`. What's the right tool?
options: Make Employee inherit from Invoice
Have both implement a shared interface, e.g. `IPayable`, with an `Amount` property
Use `object` and cast inside the loop
Copy the summing logic into both classes separately
questions.explanation: This is precisely the case interfaces solve: unrelated classes sharing a capability (having a payable amount) without a forced inheritance relationship. `List<IPayable>` lets you treat both uniformly.

questions.question: In an abstract class, what's the difference between an `abstract` method and a `virtual` method?
options: No difference
`abstract` has no body and FORCES every concrete subclass to override it; `virtual` has a default body and overriding is optional
`virtual` cannot be overridden at all
`abstract` methods can only exist in interfaces
questions.explanation: `abstract` methods end with `;` (no implementation) and every non-abstract derived class MUST override them. `virtual` methods provide a working default that derived classes MAY override if they choose.

questions.question: An interface can contain fields (like `private int _count;`).
questions.explanation: Interfaces cannot hold fields or any storage — only member signatures (methods, properties, events) that implementing classes must provide. Fields are the implementing class's responsibility.
